name: Colin Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does your working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I open the complaints queue, take the billing cases that have already bounced around, and coach new agents on what to check. I am a team lead, and the higher pay reflects the hard cases I handle, though it took years to get here after my two-year college diploma. The best part is hearing a customer breathe out when the account finally makes sense.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you have to think about at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27 and live alone, with no children. I have about nine months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of other centres nearby. That makes me less afraid for myself than I am for colleagues with a rent bill and no buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team to treat an AI summary like any other note: read it before signing your name to it. If little else changes, I would push for the time saved to go back into careful customer work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my wage and role are safe here. I have nine months saved and other centres to call if this one turns sour, but the new agents may still be squeezed by the ordinary call targets. A mild AI future does not fix a bad roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep taking difficult billing calls and check the summaries before they enter the account record. I would bring the saved minutes to our staff meeting and ask that quality checks get time on the roster. During the first year I would keep the same savings plan and the same flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own income. I still feel bothered by the way a few minutes saved can quietly become a harder target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at that staff meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the before-and-after call times and how many cases were reopened. I do not want to claim a saving if another agent has to fix the same bill tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move jobs over an ordinary target change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would raise it here first. I know the dispute rules and the people on this floor, and it would be foolish to leave a well-paid post over one bad month.

say: I would tell agents to **check summaries** before signing them.
I would ask for saved minutes to support **careful calls**.
think: I think my **wage** is safe in this mild picture.
I still worry that new agents face tougher **targets**.
do: Keep handling **billing disputes** and checking summaries.
Ask the **staff meeting** for quality time on the roster.
Keep my **savings plan** and flat during the first year.
S0.quote: A mild AI future does not fix a bad roster.
fieldNote: His nine-month **cushion** makes personal risk small.
He notices how saved time can become a harder **target**.
He would raise evidence at a **staff meeting** before considering a move.

steps.text: Keep taking difficult billing calls and checking summaries before filing them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues we need a say in how the answer system is measured. I would join the staff association meeting and ask for published figures on reopened complaints, hours and job cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think easy chats will vanish and lead teams may shrink. I could probably find another job nearby, but that does not replace the whole queue for my colleagues. My higher wage may also make me an expensive name on a staffing sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would trial the answer tool on paid time and record wrong account advice. I would join the staff association and ask it to press for retraining places with paid hours. In the first year of these changes, if my team is cut I would apply for a paid dispute review post here or at another nearby centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own job but still able to act. The combination of a reserve and nearby employers lets me speak at the meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if management calls your figures negative?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the customer cases and the second calls they caused. The figures are part of doing the job, not a vote against a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a pay cut for the review post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one might be manageable for a clear path, but I would not accept a vacancy that cannot cover my rent and bills. I would compare the posted wage before applying.

feel: **Able to act** because savings and jobs are nearby.

fieldNote: He treats AI errors as **service evidence**, not a general objection.

steps.text: Trial the answer tool on paid time and record wrong account advice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the floor that AGI by 2028 puts our screen work first, and the employer should give written notice before changing shifts. I would ask the staff association to seek a fair transition plan and funded places in jobs that remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most calls to be automated by 2028, including disputes I handle well. Robots arriving around 2031 are later, but this desk has almost no hands-on part. Nine months of savings and many nearby centres give me a route, though they may all cut hiring at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the association to press for notice and paid training tied to named roles, while I check actual dispute-review vacancies each week. I would keep my nine-month reserve intact rather than buying an unproven course. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my post ends I would take a paid review or compliance job whose wage covers my expenses; otherwise I would use the reserve while applying more widely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, especially for the people with no savings. I might lose my job, but I have enough time and money to search without taking the first bad offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a junior agent with no reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them what the association is asking for and show them posted openings, not say they will be fine. My savings cannot solve their rent problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not pay for a course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pay for one if it was required for a real vacancy and still left enough for rent. A course sold on fear, with no employer or role attached, is not a plan.

say: I would demand **written notice** before shifts change.
I would ask the **association** for a funded transition plan.
think: Most of my calls could go by **2028**.
My nine-month **reserve** helps, but nearby hiring may freeze at several centres together.
do: Ask the association for **notice** and role-linked training.
Keep my **reserve** intact before any course purchase.
S2.quote: A course sold on fear, with no employer or role attached, is not a plan.
fieldNote: He correctly separates 2028 desk work from later **robots**.
He has a real **financial bridge**, not certainty of work.
He will fund a course only for a **real vacancy** while protecting rent.

steps.text: Ask the staff association to seek notice and funded training tied to named roles
Check paid dispute review and compliance vacancies weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the staff association that five years gives us time to negotiate training places and staffing dates before anyone loses hours. I would also ask the company to publish which disputes it still needs people to settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think full AGI in 2031 can take my desk. Five years lets me build more experience in complex appeals and see where paid posts survive. I can switch employers nearby if I have to, but I would rather help set fair terms here first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would train on the appeal rules through a funded internal course if the company offers one tied to a posted role. I would keep the association involved in checking the staffing plan and save toward a full year of expenses. In the first year after 2031, if calls go I would apply for a paid appeals vacancy with a stated wage before leaving the centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, with a specific route to work on. Five years is enough to ask what the job actually is and who pays for the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lead the association work yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would attend meetings and help gather case evidence, but I would not speak for every agent alone. People on different shifts need to say what they can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no funded appeals course appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep handling appeals and checking nearby openings. I would not resign to study full time merely because someone predicts 2031.

say: I would press for **training places** and staffing dates.
I would ask which disputes still need **people** after full AGI arrives in 2031.
think: I can build appeal experience and search **nearby** over five years while keeping my wage.
do: Take a funded **appeals course** if linked to a posted role.
S3.quote: People on different shifts need to say what they can afford.
fieldNote: He prefers setting fair **terms** before seeking another employer.
The appeals course depends on **funding** and a posted role.
He would gather evidence without claiming to speak for **everyone**.

steps.text: Take a funded appeals course if the company links it to a posted paid role
Attend staff association meetings and gather case evidence for staffing discussions
Save toward one year of expenses before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team a decade gives us time to build skills and demand a say in how the firm uses them. I would ask for a written pay path for the people who test AI answers and settle appeals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 when AGI arrives in 2036, and I do not expect today's call queue to be there. I have time to move into complex appeals if it is a real paid job. Robots around 2039 do not change my screen-work deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep leading the complaints queue and ask to shadow the appeals team on paid time. I would save steadily and take an employer-funded appeals qualification if a posted role requires it. In the first year after 2036, I would apply for that paid role if it exists, or search the other nearby employers while keeping living costs covered by savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the work changing, not trapped. Ten years lets me judge the openings by their wages rather than their titles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the association to bargain over those roles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I would join its meetings on the pay path, because a written wage matters to every agent considering the move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make shadowing worth your time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid hours and actual appeal cases. I will not count an unpaid afternoon watching a screen as preparation for a new job.

I would join association meetings about **new roles**.

I can move if complex appeals offer a **real wage**.
do: Shadow the **appeals team** on paid hours.
Take a funded **qualification** if a posted role requires it.
S4.quote: I will not count an unpaid afternoon watching a screen as preparation for a new job.
fieldNote: He insists on **paid shadowing** with actual cases.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a whole floor could lose the work at once. Written notice, funded training for named jobs, and wages posted before anyone leaves the queue would help. The staff association could make sure the newest agents are heard too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would ask whether anyone counts the time spent putting a wrong machine answer right. A cheap first answer is not cheap if three people have to clean it up.

headlineQuote: A cheap first answer is not cheap if three people have to clean it up.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old** lead agent with a two-year college diploma and higher pay for his job.
He has nine months of **savings** and plenty of nearby centres, yet worries about less protected colleagues.
He uses AI **occasionally** and judges it by wrong advice and reopened cases.
He joins the **staff association** to seek notice, fair wages and funded paths into posted roles.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove most of the contact centre floor at once.
whatWouldHelp: Written **notice**, funded training for named jobs and posted wages would help agents prepare.
